content.text: q5: Option 2 'Increasing inventory to prepare for future price rises' is also a legitimate, commonly taught response to anticipated inflation (buying ahead). Two defensible answers; the explanation dismisses it with 'ties up cash', which is a trade-off, not a reason it is wrong.
q20: 'Evaluate' is not an MCQ stem; the correct option is the only long, hedged one and the three distractors use 'always'/'no impact' — guessable without knowledge. Same pattern in Q21-Q24.

p3: 'Evaluate the view that businesses should always prioritise shareholders over other stakeholders' (20 marks) is a stakeholders/objectives question (Unit 1 / Unit 3), not external influences. Marks are allocated per point rather than by levels. No case-study context although all IAL 20-markers are data-response. Not linked to any block.

Zero recall exercises across 12 subsections and zero diagrams: Learn Mode for this section is pure reading plus one MCQ per block. Obvious candidates omitted: reorder on the interest-rate transmission chain (rate rise → loan cost up → investment delayed / mortgage cost up → spending down → revenue down), reorder of business-cycle phases, fillin on SPICED, and a business-cycle diagram.

Inline quiz mapping is wrong for every block: Inflation block quizIndices=[0] shows the exchange-rate SPICED MCQ; Exchange/Interest/Tax block quizIndices=[1] shows the recession/luxury-cars MCQ; Business Cycle block quizIndices=[2] shows the interest-rate MCQ; Legislation block quizIndices=[3] shows patents; Competitive Environment block quizIndices=[4] shows the CMA. A student is quizzed on material from a different (sometimes not-yet-read) block.

Inline practice mapping is also wrong: Business Cycle block practiceIndices=[1] is the interest-rates 6-marker; Competitive Environment block practiceIndices=[2] is the environmental-legislation 10-marker. Practice 3 (20-mark stakeholders) and practice 4 (Outline inflation) are attached to no block, so the Inflation block has no written practice even though practice[4] is about inflation.

Only 5 of 25 MCQs are ever surfaced inline; 20 are seen only in the pre-test/post-test lottery. The five hedged 'Evaluate/To what extent' MCQs (Q20-24) can appear in the 3-question pre-test and are guessable, inflating pre-test scores.

Difficulty ramp: the section opens with Economics theory (CPI, cost-push vs demand-pull) before the business-relevant chain, and Block 4 escalates into market-structure taxonomy and Porter's Five Forces — both beyond WBS12 — while the simpler, examinable 'changes in competitive environment → business responses' is never explicitly taught.

Block 1 bundles three spec items (exchange rates, interest rates, taxation) so step 2 is 'taxation' alone with the 'spaced' recall slot unused; Block 3 'Business Legislation' covers only 2 of the 5 spec legislation areas (consumer, employee) yet quiz/practice test environmental and competition law.

Takeaways match their blocks (good), but Block 4 has four takeaways of which two ('Market structure ranges from perfect competition to monopoly', 'Porter's Five Forces reveals all competitive pressures') summarise off-spec material.

Misconceptions: 'inflation is always bad', 'a strong pound is good', 'higher interest rates always bad', 'recessions bad for all', 'legislation just increases costs' are genuine student errors. 'Businesses should pay as little tax as possible by moving abroad' (taxation), 'more competition is always better for consumers' (market-structure) and 'barriers to entry are always created deliberately' (barriers) read as filler/moralising rather than observed misconceptions.

Flow blocks: the cost-push flow ('Oil or raw material prices spike → ...') duplicates the inflation flow in the previous subsection; the business-cycle flow is a good candidate for a diagram rather than a text chain.
Taxation AND government spending — the effect of changes in government spending (public contracts, infrastructure, subsidies, austerity) on businesses is not taught at all.
The effect of economic uncertainty on the business environment — only touched in extras.evaluation ('Economic cycles are difficult to predict'); no content subsection.
Legislation: environmental protection — absent from content although quiz Q9/Q21 and practice[2] test it.
Legislation: competition law — absent from content although quiz Q4/Q14 test it (and IAL would frame it generically, not as the CMA).
Legislation: health and safety — absent entirely (content, quiz, practice, flashcards).
Competitive environment: competition and market size — market size (value/volume, growth, saturation) and its effect on a business is not taught.

Competitive environment: the effect on businesses of changes in the competitive environment (new entrants, price wars, mergers, disruptive substitutes) and typical business responses — only implicitly via the Netflix example; no explicit treatment.
Note: exact IAL sub-numbering (2.3.5 vs GCE 2.5) — unsure; the bullet content above reflects the IAL Business 'External influences' topic as far as I know it.

Add a third block 'Corporate influences' teaching short-termism vs long-termism (timescales, quarterly reporting, R&D/training cuts) and evidence-based vs subjective decision-making, so spec 3.4.1 is covered and practice Q3 is no longer testing untaught content.

content.text: Zero recall widgets (no reorder, no fillin) — the section never exercises retrieval inside Learn Mode; the 'spaced'/'immediate' recall mechanism is idle here. Natural fillin candidates: Handy's four types with their distinguishing feature; Mendelow's four quadrant strategies; Friedman/Freeman positions.

Zero diagrams although stakeholder-analysis > examMatters tells students to 'draw the 2x2 grid' — Mendelow's matrix and Handy's typology are both obvious diagram candidates; Learn Mode's InlineDiagram slot is empty for both blocks.
Blocks carry no quizIndices/practiceIndices, so which MCQ/practice item lands under each block is left to default selection; e.g. block 1 (culture/stakeholders) could surface the greenwashing MCQ.

Misconception quality: corporate-culture ('managers can switch culture overnight') and business-ethics ('ethics always costs with no return') are real; stakeholder-analysis ('Mendelow is static') is filler — the genuinely common student error ('strong culture is always good', which appears in notes[0] and common_mistakes[1]) is not in content[] at all; CSR misconception overclaims (see accuracy).

Difficulty ramp: every subsection is definitional + for/against list; evaluation is described ('examiners want both sides') but never modelled with a worked exam paragraph or a judgement criterion ('it depends on…'), which is what separates L3/L4 in IAL mark schemes.

Takeaways: Block 1 takeaways match its sections. Block 2 takeaway[2] (Friedman vs Freeman) references block 1 content — acceptable cross-link but block 2 lacks a takeaway on the profit/ethics trade-off which is the spec's core point.

(Norway has an EEA arrangement)'. Under the EU-UK TCA (2021) UK-origin goods including Scottish salmon are tariff-free and quota-free; what changed is non-tariff barriers (customs declarations, export health certificates). Norway's EEA membership excludes fisheries and Norwegian salmon actually pays an EU tariff, so this is not trade diversion caused by a CET at all. content[1] 'Cultural Influences on Global Marketing' > hofstede-dimensions > realExample: The KFC 'eat your fingers off' story is an unverified marketing legend (hedged with 'reportedly' but then built on as fact). More importantly it is presented as the Hofstede example yet applies no Hofstede dimension; it invokes 'high-context' (Edward Hall's framework, not Hofstede's) and asserts a translation error was inappropriate 'in a collectivist culture', which is a non-sequitur. Students copying this into an exam would show confused theory.

q2: Two options are defensible. Sachets are a packaging/size change (Product) that enables a lower price point (Price); Edexcel textbooks describe sachet strategies under product adaptation as often as under pricing. The explanation itself says 'by selling smaller quantities' (a product change). correctIndex=1 (Price) will be marked wrong for a student who reasonably answers Product.

Zero recall exercises (0 reorder, 0 fillin) and 0 diagrams: with 2 blocks of 2 sections each, Learn Mode is exactly 2 steps, each of which is read, read, one MCQ, one written question, explain-it-back, takeaway. No spaced/immediate recall widgets fire at all.

Quiz/content mismatch: 5 of 10 MCQs (indices 1,3,4,6,8) examine terms never taught in content[] (ethnocentric/polycentric/geocentric, Ansoff, Porter, niche markets). The PreTest draws 3 random items from this bank, so roughly half of pretests will contain untaught material, which directly feeds the founder's 'pre-test demotivates' hypothesis.

Block 1 'Standardisation vs Adaptation' has sections on standardisation and glocalisation only; the spec's three named approaches (domestic/ethnocentric, mixed/geocentric, international/polycentric) are the examinable vocabulary and are absent, while takeaway[1] summarises an 'Adaptation' section that does not exist.

Block 2 spends one of two sections on Hofstede (off-spec) and compresses six spec bullets (language, unintended meanings, translations, branding/promotion, social media, different tastes) into one section; social media is never mentioned anywhere in content[].

Section is numbered 4.3.3 and titled 'Global Marketing', but in the IAL WBS14 spec 4.3 is the topic ('Global marketing') with 4.3.1 Marketing, 4.3.2 Niche markets, 4.3.3 Cultural/social factors. The content spans 4.3.1 and 4.3.3 but the numbering suggests only the latter; niche markets (4.3.2) exist only in flashcards/quiz/practice/extras.

Misconceptions: global-standardisation ('always cheaper') and cultural-mistakes-brand-impact ('only translations') are genuine student errors. glocalisation's misconception ('simple middle ground') is filler: it is an assertion that glocalisation is 'harder, not easier' rather than a correction of something students actually write. hofstede-dimensions' is plausible but concerns an off-spec framework.

No 'realExample' or body text provides a verified language/translation/branding failure inside content[]; the only such examples are in flashcards (Nova, mythical) and the KFC anecdote, so the spec bullets most likely to appear in a 4/6-marker have the thinnest, least reliable evidence.

Difficulty ramp is flat rather than sensible: both steps are at the same descriptive level; there is no progression from definitions (approaches) to application (4Ps decisions) to strategic frameworks (Ansoff/Porter) to evaluation, even though the quiz and practice assume the last two.

content.text: Add a block on effects of change (competitiveness, productivity, financial performance, stakeholders) and key factors in successful change (organisational culture, size, speed of change, transformational leadership) plus Kotter & Schlesinger's six strategies, so that quiz indices 0,2,3,4,5,6,7,8 and practice index 3 test material the lesson actually teaches; then set quizIndices/practiceIndices per block.

Fix the disruptive/step conflation: rename the type-of-change pair to incremental vs step (transformational) change across content, notes and flashcards; treat disruption as an external cause; reword the section-1 examMatters that tells firms to 'use disruptive change'.

Add recall widgets and a diagram: a reorder recall for Kotter's 8 steps (genuine procedural sequence; use one consistent wording), a fillin for Lewin's driving/restraining forces, and an InlineDiagram of a force field so the 'draw the diagram' advice is backed by one. Move the Toyota example to section 1 and replace the duplicate Nadella example.

Bring practice questions to IAL form: contextual 'Explain one reason... (4)' instead of 'Explain two'; convert the 6-mark Analyse to an 8-mark Assess; anchor the 10- and 20-mark stems to the bank / insurance company; replace the off-spec crisis-management question with a succession-planning or business-continuity question.

Types of Change > incremental-vs-disruptive-change > examMatters ('use disruptive change when external forces ... make the current model unsustainable'): Conflates two different concepts. The body defines disruptive change as something that 'comes from outside the established players' and 'destroys incumbents' (Christensen), i.e. a market phenomenon done TO a firm. examMatters then tells the student the firm should 'use disruptive change' as a management choice. A firm cannot 'use' disruption; it undertakes step/transformational change in response to it. The notes[] compound this with 'Disruptive (step) change' and the flashcards switch to 'transformational change', so three vocabularies for one idea.

Types of Change > drivers-and-scenario-planning > body paragraph 3, flow, keyIdea, misconception; notes[2] 'Scenario Planning': 'Scenario planning' is taught as Shell-style strategic foresight (2-4 futures, best/worst/most-likely/wildcard). In IAL 3.6.3 the heading 'Scenario planning' means identifying key risks through risk assessment (natural disasters, IT failure, loss of key staff), planning for risk mitigation (business continuity, succession planning) and the costs/benefits of contingency planning. A student who answers a 3.6.3 question with Shell scenarios will miss the indicative content entirely. The section's own quiz (Q5, Q6, Q9), flashcards (contingency, business continuity, succession, COVID) and practice Q4 use the spec meaning, so the lesson contradicts its own assessment items.

content.text: q2: Tests Kotter & Schlesinger's six strategies (education/communication, participation, facilitation, negotiation, manipulation/co-optation, coercion), which the content[] never teaches; the lesson teaches Kotter's 8-STEP model, so students will conflate the two Kotters. Answer itself (coercion) is fine as textbook framing, though K&S actually say coercion is appropriate when speed is essential.

q5: Odd wording: 'inadequate business continuity planning' is a weakness, not a risk, and 'MOST significant' is opinion with no case context. Business continuity planning is also never taught in content[] (only in flashcards). Distractors (poor marketing, excessive diversification) are nonsense for the stem.

Content/assessment mismatch is the core defect: 8 of 10 quiz MCQs (indices 0,2,3,4,5,6,7,8) and practice index 3 test spec content (Handy cultures, Kotter & Schlesinger, transformational leadership, succession planning, business continuity, size of organisation, contingency-planning costs) that the content[] blocks never teach. The PreTest draws 3 random MCQs from this bank, so most students will be pre-tested on things the lesson then ignores, and the PostTest 'improvement' is noise.

Zero recall widgets (0 reorder, 0 fillin) in a section that contains the best genuine sequence in the whole unit: Kotter's 8 steps. Also no fillin for Lewin's driving/restraining forces. Learn Mode steps therefore have no retrieval practice beyond one MCQ per block.

Zero diagrams, yet managing-change-models > examMatters instructs students to 'Draw Lewin's force field diagram'. A force field diagram (driving arrows vs restraining arrows on a line marked 'current state') is the obvious InlineDiagram and would also make the 'reduce restraining forces' insight concrete.

Only 2 blocks x 2 sections = 2 Learn Mode steps for an entire spec topic (3.6.1-3.6.3). No block covers effects of change, key factors in successful change (culture, size, speed) or risk/contingency planning. Suggested structure: Block 1 Causes and types of change; Block 2 Effects and key factors (culture, size, speed, leadership); Block 3 Managing resistance (K&S strategies + Lewin + Kotter); Block 4 Scenario/contingency planning (risk assessment, business continuity, succession, cost/benefit).

content[0] 'MNC Impact & Ethics' > mnc-negative-impacts-ethics > body[0]: 'In extreme cases, repatriated profits exceed the original investment, making the host country a net loser.' This is a fallacy: any profitable long-lived investment eventually returns more than its initial capital; that does not make the host a net loser because the host retains wages, supplier spending, tax and capital stock. It teaches a common student error as fact.

q2: Rana Plaza appears nowhere in content[] (only flashcards[1] and common_mistakes). Because PreTest samples 3 random MCQs from this bank and InlineQuiz draws from it, students are examined on material Learn Mode never teaches.
q3: Greenwashing is not taught in content[] (flashcards only). Same untaught-material problem; and it duplicates Q9's concept, so 2 of 10 questions test one term that is not in the lesson.
q5: 'Controlling MNCs' is entirely absent from content[]. Also the stem gives the answer away: 'organisations ... campaigning' maps directly onto 'Pressure group activism'; no thinking required.

p4: 'Evaluate whether the growth of MNCs has been a positive or negative development for the global economy' — 20 marks with context: null. IAL Business 20-mark questions are always data-response, framed around a specific business/country decision in the extract ('Evaluate whether X should...' / 'Evaluate the likely impact of ... on Y'). A context-free 'global economy' essay is an Economics-style framing and cannot earn IAL application marks. Guidance is an unranked pro/con list with no levelled scheme (Level 4 = balanced, contextual judgement) and no model answer.

Zero recall widgets (0 reorder, 0 fillin) and 0 diagrams: with block 1 = 2 sections and block 2 = 2 sections, the whole Learn Mode is exactly 2 steps of ~700-800 words of prose each, followed by one InlineQuiz MCQ, one practice question, ExplainItBack and a takeaway. There is no spaced/immediate recall at all, so the section is the passive-reading failure mode the founder worries about (opposite of the 'arbitrary reorder' problem).

Transfer pricing is taught twice: content[0] > mnc-negative-impacts-ethics > body[2] (full mechanism, components example) and content[1] > transfer-pricing-mechanism (full mechanism again, brand-name example, BEPS). The avoidance-vs-evasion misconception is also repeated in notes[1]. Block 2 section 2 (fdi-stakeholder-analysis) then re-sorts block 1's positives/negatives by stakeholder, so roughly half of block 2 is restatement.

No difficulty ramp and no foundation: 'FDI', 'MNC' and 'subsidiary' are used from the first sentence without definition; 'arm's length' is defined only in block 2 after transfer pricing has already been explained in block 1. All four sections sit at the same evaluative level ('net impact depends on governance') rather than definitions -> mechanisms -> evaluation.

Content[] vs assessment misalignment: quiz (6/10 items), flashcards (10/19), common_mistakes (4/6) and extras chains cover controlling MNCs, greenwashing, Rana Plaza, Nestlé, boycotts, social media — none of which appear in content[]. PreTest and InlineQuiz therefore examine students on material the lesson never presents, which is a plausible driver of pre-test demotivation.

examMatters is near-identical across all four sections (variations of 'the net impact depends on the host country's governance capacity, the MNC's industry and the regulatory framework'); the block 2 takeaway[3] repeats block 1 takeaway[2]. The evaluation template is good but repeated four times it reads as filler.

Misconceptions: 'Students assume MNCs always benefit host countries' (mnc-positive-impacts) and 'Students assume all MNCs deliberately exploit host countries' (mnc-negative-impacts-ethics) are mirror images and generic; only the avoidance/evasion and host-only-stakeholder ones are genuine, mark-scheme-relevant errors.

Block 1 title 'MNC Impact & Ethics' promises ethics, but ethics content is one sentence on labour exploitation and one on pollution havens; marketing ethics, child labour and stakeholder conflict (all spec bullets) are absent. Block 2 title 'Transfer Pricing & FDI Stakeholders' bundles two unrelated topics.

Economics framing leaks into a Business section ('current account', 'multiplier effects', 'resource curse', 'global economy' in the 20-marker); IAL Business examiners want business-decision and stakeholder framing.

content[0] 'The Supply Curve' > supply-and-the-supply-curve > realExample: Saudi Arabia is presented as raising output above $80 'because expensive extraction methods become profitable' and cutting drilling when prices fell below $30 in early 2016. Saudi Arabia has the lowest lifting costs in the world (roughly $3-10/bbl) and its output is set by OPEC/political strategy; in 2014-16 it famously INCREASED production to record levels (~10.5m bpd) to defend market share while prices collapsed. The example describes US shale/oil-sands behaviour and attributes it to the wrong producer; a student who repeats it in an exam is writing something a well-informed examiner knows is false.

content[2] 'Short Run vs Long Run' (whole block: short-run-production, long-run-production-and-returns-to-scale, takeaway): Diminishing marginal returns, marginal product, and increasing/constant/decreasing returns to scale are WEC13 (Unit 3, business behaviour: costs and economies of scale) content. The WEC11 supply/PES bullet only requires 'the distinction between short run and long run and its significance for elasticity of supply'. The block never mentions PES or elasticity at all, so it teaches the wrong exam use of the SR/LR distinction and tells Unit 1 students that examiners 'set trap questions' on returns-to-scale terminology in this topic.

q21: correctIndex 0 ('market price exceeds its average total costs') is wrong or at best contestable. A firm continues to supply in the short run as long as price covers average VARIABLE cost (shut-down rule) and produces where P = MC; option 1 ('price is at least equal to its marginal cost') is the textbook supply condition for a price-taking firm. P > ATC is the long-run break-even condition, and a firm with P < ATC but P > AVC still supplies. This is WEC13 Unit 3 theory-of-the-firm content anyway and has no place in a WEC11 supply bank; it can be drawn into the PreTest at random.
content.evidence: audit/snapshots/2026-09-11-post-packet-0__economics__supply.json quiz[21].correctIndex changed 0->1 and explanation now states the short-run supply condition is P=MC, shutdown at AVC, not ATC

content.text: p0: 'Define the term price elasticity of supply (4 marks)'. (b) Guidance lists Help to Buy (demand-side) as a supply factor. (c) Entirely UK-specific (green belt, London, Help to Buy) for an international-school cohort who will get contexts like Malaysian palm oil or Vietnamese rice; no data extract is provided though such a question in WEC11 would be data-response.

Public Goods > characteristics-public-goods (body para 4) and block takeaway 'Private markets produce zero public goods — complete failure': Absolutist claim that the free market provides 'zero quantity' of public goods. The IAL spec wording is 'why public goods MAY NOT be provided by the private sector'. The section's own common_mistakes[2] ('Saying public goods cannot be provided by the market') says this exact claim is a mistake and that the issue is under-provision. Internal contradiction that a student will be marked down for repeating.

Public Goods > characteristics-public-goods > realExample (UK lighthouse system): States lighthouses were 'historically funded by the government' and that Trinity House 'collects dues from ports rather than individual vessels'. Historically English lighthouses were largely privately built and financed by light dues levied on ships (Coase 1974 uses this as the canonical counterexample of private provision of a public good); today light dues are charged per ship tonnage on vessels calling at UK/Irish ports into the General Lighthouse Fund, not general taxation. The example undermines the point it is meant to make and is factually wrong.

Welfare Loss & Deadweight Loss > measuring-welfare-loss (body para 1): 'In a perfectly competitive market, total surplus is maximised at the equilibrium where supply meets demand. Any deviation from this point — whether through externalities, monopoly power, or government intervention — reduces total surplus.' With an externality the market equilibrium is NOT the surplus-maximising point; the externality is a property of that equilibrium, not a deviation from it, and moving away from it (a Pigouvian tax) raises welfare. This contradicts the whole Externalities block and the practice[3] model answer.

Externalities > negative-externalities-consumption > examMatters: 'Examiners penalise students who draw MSC above MPC for a consumption externality.' Edexcel/IAL mark schemes for demerit-good/cigarette questions routinely accept an external-cost (MSC > MPC) diagram; the IAL spec only requires diagrams for external costs of production and external benefits of consumption. Telling students they will be penalised for the diagram most mark schemes list is misleading about marking.

Every one of the 8 reorder recalls is the subsection's own flow box (steps + result) verbatim, and the 'immediate' recall renders at the bottom of the same step where that flow box is visible. All 8 fillins carry first-letters+underscore hints that make the blank one-option; 5 hints have the wrong length (allocative-inefficiency 'un____________', free-rider 'ex_________' and 'ta_______', demerit 'ex____________', diagrams-welfare-loss 'un____________' and 'co__________').

Redundant coverage: 'allocative-inefficiency-deadweight-loss' (block 1) and 'measuring-welfare-loss' + 'diagrams-welfare-loss' (block 7) teach the same deadweight-loss idea three times, with block 1 introducing DWL before the student has seen a single externality diagram. Merge block 7 into block 2 (externality welfare loss) and cut block 1 to a definition + the three spec types.

Difficulty ramp/spec fit: blocks 4 (merit/demerit), 5b (moral hazard/adverse selection) and 6 (monopoly) are Unit 3/4 or non-Edexcel material yet sit in the middle of the Unit 1 section; a WEC11 student is told 'examiners expect you to draw a monopoly diagram', which is not examined in Unit 1. Meanwhile the spec's 1.3.4 'symmetric vs asymmetric information' and 1.3.3 'public vs private goods' get no subsection.

2-per-step pairing is coherent (neg prod + neg cons; pos prod + pos cons; merit + demerit; then info failure alone; asymmetric + moral hazard; monopoly alone; measuring + diagrams). No pairing breaks a concept.

Takeaways mostly match their blocks; exceptions: Public Goods takeaway 'Private markets produce zero public goods — complete failure' contradicts common_mistakes[2]; Externalities takeaway 'Government uses taxes and subsidies to close the gap' is the only mention of intervention in a block that otherwise never teaches it.

Misconceptions: most are genuine (public goods = government-provided; education is a public good; merit vs public; moral hazard vs adverse selection; DWL vs fall in consumer surplus; allocative vs productive inefficiency). Filler-ish: 'negative externalities only come from pollution', 'information failure only affects uneducated consumers', 'free riding = laziness', 'monopolies are always bad' (the last is Unit 3 evaluation, not a Unit 1 misconception).

Pre-test gate draws 3 random MCQs from a 25-item bank that contains a wrongly keyed item (Q18), four near-duplicate pairs and two untaught topics (Q20, Q22); a student can be told they were wrong for a correct answer before the lesson even starts.
1.3.4(a) 'distinction between symmetric and asymmetric information' — symmetric information is never defined or contrasted; only asymmetric is taught.
1.3.3(a) 'distinction between public goods and private goods' — private goods (rival, excludable) are never defined; quasi-public goods / common resources are not taught although quiz Q20 tests them.

1.3.2(a)/(b) explicit 'private cost + external cost = social cost' and 'private benefit + external benefit = social benefit' relationships are only in common_mistakes[0] and quiz Q16, never stated as a taught formula in a subsection body.
1.3.2(d) welfare GAIN from correcting a positive consumption externality (spec wording covers welfare loss and gain areas); content only ever calls the positive-externality triangle a 'welfare loss'.

Unit 1 numbering: the app labels this '1.3.5 Market Failure'; in the 2018 IAL spec market failure is 1.3.1-1.3.4 (types, externalities, public goods, information gaps) — unsure of the app's mapping convention; worth checking that 1.3.1-1.3.4 are not double-covered elsewhere.

Not spec gaps but over-coverage worth flagging: merit/demerit goods (not Edexcel terminology in IAL Unit 1), monopoly as market failure (WEC13 Unit 3), moral hazard/adverse selection (WEC14 Unit 4 financial market failure).

Re-map quizIndices to block content (e.g. block0 [0,12,14,23]; block1 [6,15,9]; block2 [1,10]; block3 [2,11,17]; block4 [3,16]; block5 [8,20,24]; block6 [7,19]; block7 [4,5,13,18,22]) and fix practiceIndices so each block gets its own question — either index the marks-sorted array deliberately or remove the sort in LearnModeTab.jsx:82 before indexing. Put the essay on block 7.

Change block 0 diagramRef from 'Indirect Tax' to a string contained in the diagram title (e.g. 'Tax to Correct') so the tax diagram renders; consider adding a specific-vs-ad-valorem supply-shift diagram.

Stop reorder recalls duplicating the on-screen flow: either render the first section's recall only as a spaced recall on the next step, or rewrite the nine reorders as longer chains (incidence, revenue, elasticity, Pc/Pp) that are not visible above. Replace the three weak reorders (direct-state-provision, types-of-regulation, examples-and-evaluation) with the free-rider chain, a classification exercise, and a scenario judgement.

Fix practice mark allocations to WEC11 format: 20-mark Evaluate -> 14-mark 'Discuss'/'Evaluate' with a KAA/Evaluation level split in the guidance; 4-mark Define -> 2-mark Define or 4-mark 'Explain, with an example'; 'Outline' -> 'Explain'. Rewrite guidance as levels, not point sums.

Correct the factual/IAL-fit issues: London taxi example (no numeric cap), MUP '13% in the first year', plug-in grant 'up to £1,500', 'UK airline deregulation', nudge-theory exam claim; add the spec-named government-failure causes (distortion of price signals, excessive administrative costs) and swap several UK examples for international ones.

Government Failure > examples-and-evaluation-of-government-failure > realExample: Claims London taxi licensing 'restricted the number of black cabs', 'keeping fares high and limiting supply'. London has never numerically capped black-cab licences (the constraint is the Knowledge test; fares are set by TfL). The capped-medallion case is New York, not London. Students citing this in an exam would be citing a false fact.

State Provision > information-provision-and-nudge-theory > examMatters: 'Nudge theory is increasingly popular in exam questions ... libertarian paternalism' — nudge theory and libertarian paternalism are not in the IAL WEC11 specification (1.2.10 covers habitual behaviour, influence of others, computational weakness). This is UK GCE-flavoured content presented as an IAL exam expectation.
content.note: SPEC NUMBERING: this item cites 1.2.10, which is UK GCE A-level numbering and does not exist in the IAL spec. The IAL topic for this section is 1.3.6. Find the requirement by its wording in audit/raw/econ_spec.txt, not by the number. (noted 13 Sep 2026)

content.text: p3: 'Evaluate ... (20 marks)' — 20-mark essays are WEC13/WEC14 (Unit 3/4) format. WEC11 Section B tops out at 14 marks (Discuss/Evaluate). Guidance is also point-allocated (2+3+2+2+2+2+2+1+2+2) whereas IAL uses levels-based KAA + Evaluation marking. In addition this question is never surfaced in Learn Mode because practiceIndices only reach sorted positions 0-3.

quizIndices are sequential [0]..[7] and do not match block content: block 'Subsidies' shows Q1 (maximum price), 'Maximum Prices' shows Q2 (minimum price on alcohol), 'Minimum Prices' shows Q3 (permits vs tax), 'Tradeable Pollution Permits' shows Q4 (government failure definition), 'State Provision' shows Q5 (rent controls as government failure), 'Regulation' shows Q6 (vaccination subsidy). Only blocks 0 (Q0 tax) and 7 (Q7 regulatory capture) are on-topic. Six of eight inline quizzes are off-topic.

practiceIndices are applied to a marks-sorted copy of practice[] (LearnModeTab.jsx:82 sortedPractice, :110-113), so the data indices [0],[1],[2],[3] resolve to: block 'Subsidies' -> 'Define government failure' (worked mode), 'Minimum Prices' -> 'Outline two disadvantages of a maximum price' (guided), 'State Provision' -> 'Explain two ways indirect taxes correct market failure' (guided), 'Government Failure' -> 'Assess subsidies' (independent). Every inline practice is in the wrong block, and the 20-mark essay never appears. Either the data must index the sorted array deliberately or the code must stop sorting before indexing.

diagramRef 'Indirect Tax' on block 0 never matches diagram title 'Tax to Correct Negative Externality' (LearnModeTab.jsx:97-104 requires one string to contain the other), so the tax diagram — the one the section's examMatters says 'examiners expect you to draw' — is never rendered in Learn Mode. The other three refs (Subsidy, Maximum Price, Minimum Price) match.

All nine reorder recalls are verbatim copies of the flow widget in the same section's body, and because each is the first section of its step they render as 'immediate' recalls at the bottom of the same step with the flow visible above. Students can copy the order from the screen; the reorder score in CompletionScreen is therefore meaningless for this section.

Fill-in recalls are a three-word drag bank (FillInRecall.jsx:12). With three grammatically distinct slots, six of eight are solved by grammar without economics. 'Complete the chain:' is used for lists that are not chains (price floors: income/store/wage; causes of government failure: imperfect/short-termism/capture).
Six hint strings are one character longer than the answer (opportunity, information, architecture, competition, imperfect, short-termism) — cosmetic but signals unreviewed generation.

Step structure is monotone: nine steps, each 'How X works' + 'Evaluating X' + MCQ + takeaway + explain-back. There is no ramp; every policy tool is treated at the same depth, and the section never asks students to choose between tools for a given market failure (the actual IAL 12/14-mark skill) until the final block.

Real examples are almost entirely UK (tobacco duty, sugar levy, plug-in grant, NHS, National Minimum Wage, Scotland MUP, UK auto-enrolment, UK buses/airlines, London taxis). For an IAL cohort in HK/SG/MY/PK/LK/Middle East, IAL papers use international contexts; examples like Singapore COE, Malaysian/Indonesian fuel subsidies, India MSP floors, Pakistan wheat support prices, HK public housing would land better.

Misconception filler: 'Maximum Prices > effects-and-evaluation-of-price-ceilings > misconception' ('students assume the government should set it closer to equilibrium') describes a legitimate trade-off, not a misconception; the text concedes the point. Most other misconceptions are genuine (permits 'rich firms pollute as much as they want', 'subsidies always better than taxes', 'information always works').

Block 7 pairing: step 8 = 'What is government failure' + 'Causes'; step 9 = 'Examples and Evaluation' alone. Coherent, but step 9 is where the 20-mark essay should sit and it currently receives 'Assess subsidies' instead.
Takeaways match their blocks. Block 2 takeaway 'Subsidies may achieve affordability without creating shortages' is only supported by one sentence of examMatters, not the body.

Government failure causes named in the IAL spec: 'distortion of price signals' is never stated as a cause (the section lists imperfect information, political short-termism, regulatory capture, unintended consequences); 'excessive administrative costs' is only mentioned in passing in examples-and-evaluation, not taught as a cause.

Tax incidence on consumers vs producers (specific and ad valorem) is referenced in examMatters and tested in Q23 but never taught; the section needs at least a cross-reference to 1.2.9 or a short incidence paragraph tied to the tax diagram's Pc/Pp labels.
content.note: SPEC NUMBERING: this item cites 1.2.9, which is UK GCE A-level numbering and does not exist in the IAL spec. The IAL topic for this section is 1.3.6. Find the requirement by its wording in audit/raw/econ_spec.txt, not by the number. (noted 13 Sep 2026)

content.text: Specific vs ad valorem taxes: mentioned in one sentence (parallel vs pivotal shift) with no diagram; the spec expects students to draw both.
Minimum price on demerit goods vs indirect tax comparison (who receives the extra revenue: retailers vs government) — a standard IAL evaluation point, absent.

Choosing between interventions for a given market failure (e.g. tax vs regulation vs permits for pollution; subsidy vs state provision vs information for a merit good) is only partially covered in permits and regulation examMatters; no dedicated comparison content.

Spec numbering: unsure whether IAL 2018 places government failure under 1.3.6 or a separate point; the section merges both, which is defensible, but worth confirming against the WEC11 specification document.
Buffer stock schemes appear in the quiz (Q21) but are not in the section and, as far as I recall, not in the 2018 IAL WEC11 spec — unsure; if they are, they need teaching; if not, remove Q21.

Add tax and subsidy diagrams (specific parallel shift, ad valorem pivot, consumer/producer incidence shares, tax revenue rectangle, subsidy cost rectangle) and give them titles that the diagramRef substring match will find ('Indirect Tax', 'Subsidy'), so Blocks 4 and 5 stop rendering with no diagram.

Rebuild practice[] to the IAL Appendix 6 tariffs (Define 2 / Explain 4 / Draw 4 / Calculate 2-4 / Analyse 6 / Examine 8 / Discuss 14 / Evaluate 20): delete the UK oil-price macro essay and the 'Outline' price-floor item, add a Calculate on incidence/revenue, a Draw on a subsidy, and an Examine/Discuss on the price mechanism across local/national/global markets; make practiceIndices index practice[] (not the marks-sorted copy) so each block gets an on-topic question.

Fix the recall layer: give every fillin a word bank with distractors (elastic/inelastic, up/down, left/right, demand/supply, original/new) and remove first-letter hints; replace the five non-sequence reorders (equilibrium slopes, producer surplus $150/$200, three price-mechanism functions, tax welfare areas, subsidy evaluation) with classification or diagram-area drills.

Teach the missing spec bullets - 3b price mechanism in local, national and global markets (with Asian/Middle-East examples) and 2b effect of demand/supply shifts on CS and PS - then re-key Q14 to the standard answer; move Block 6 to 1.3.2 and re-key it to the spec's own list (herding, habit, inertia, poor computation, need to feel valued, framing/bias).

Correct or replace the wrong/dated examples (London 'rent controls', CBO sugar-tax score, Glastonbury resale, 59p fuel duty, pre-2003 CAP) and de-UK the examples for the HK/SG/MY/PK audience; fix quizIndices so the CS/PS block shows Q6 and the Subsidies block shows a subsidy MCQ.

Equilibrium Price & Quantity > excess-demand-and-excess-supply > realExample: Claims London has 'rent controls' that keep supply below equilibrium. Private-sector rent control in England was abolished by the Housing Act 1988; London rents are market-set. Also 'many are outbid' describes price adjusting upward, which contradicts the claim of below-equilibrium pricing.

Consumer Surplus & Producer Surplus > total-welfare-and-efficiency > realExample: 'The US Congressional Budget Office estimates deadweight loss when scoring tax proposals. A proposed sugar tax...' - CBO scores federal legislation and does not publish deadweight-loss triangles in scores; there is no federal sugar-tax score of this kind. Worse, the example contradicts the paragraph's own misconception text: a sugar tax targets a negative externality, so it can raise, not reduce, total welfare.

q14: Keyed answer 'ambiguous' conflicts with (a) the section's own teaching ('When the price rises, consumer surplus shrinks' in consumer-surplus body[1], which points students to 'decreases') and (b) the standard IAL answer for spec bullet 2b: with a rightward demand shift and upward-sloping supply, the CS triangle under the new demand curve is larger, so CS rises. Three contradictory signals on a spec-listed point.

p3: 'Evaluate the impact of a significant increase in global oil prices on the UK economy (20 marks)' is a Unit 2 (WEC12) macro essay: the guidance is entirely cost-push inflation, real disposable income, GDP growth and Bank of England monetary policy - none of it taught in 1.3.4, and UK-specific for international students. The 20-mark tariff itself matches IAL 'Evaluate', but the guidance is point-marked ('3 marks', '2 marks') whereas IAL 20-markers are levels-marked (KAA + evaluation levels).
content.evidence: audit/snapshots/2026-09-11-post-packet-0__economics__price-determination.json practice[3].hidden=true (UK oil-price WEC12 macro essay), withheld via isPracticeVisible

content.text: p2: 'Assess the effectiveness of the price mechanism... (10 marks)': 'Assess' is not an IAL Economics command word (spec Appendix 6 lists Define 2, Calculate 2/4, Draw 4, Explain 4, Analyse 6, Examine 8, Discuss 14, Evaluate 20) and there is no 10-mark tariff in WEC11. The guidance is point-marked, not levels-marked. Should be 'Examine... (8)' or 'Discuss... (14)', ideally with reference to an extract, and should mention local/national/global markets (spec 3b).

p4: 'Outline two effects of a price floor set above the equilibrium price (4 marks)': 'Outline' is not an IAL command word, and price floors/minimum wage are 1.3.6 Government intervention, not taught in this section's content (only flashcards mention them). Model answer's 'government may need to purchase surplus output' is fine but off-topic here.

p2: Bank-level gap: none of the five questions covers indirect taxes, subsidies, incidence, or CS/PS (half the spec bullets), and there is no Calculate or Draw question despite the QS requirement (>=20% of marks) and the topic being the most diagram-heavy in Unit 1. Additionally LearnModeTab.jsx:80/113 indexes practiceIndices into the marks-sorted list, so Block 3 (Price Mechanism) shows the price-floor question and Block 4 (Indirect Taxes) shows the excess-supply question; the Assess and Evaluate items never appear inline.

No diagram renders for the Indirect Taxes or Subsidies blocks: diagramRef 'Indirect Tax' and 'Subsidy' are matched by substring against diagram titles ('Supply & Demand Equilibrium', 'Consumer & Producer Surplus') in LearnModeTab.jsx:97-104, so neither matches; and no tax/subsidy/incidence/DWL SVG exists anywhere in diagrams[]. Meanwhile examMatters in three subsections tells students tax/subsidy diagrams are compulsory.

Inline quiz mismatch: quizIndices [1] puts Q1 (increase in demand) on the Consumer/Producer Surplus block instead of Q6; quizIndices [4] puts Q4 (cigarette tax incidence) on the Subsidies block instead of Q5/Q13/Q20; the Alternative Views block has no quizIndices although Q7 (bounded rationality) exists.

Inline practice mismatch (practiceIndices index the marks-sorted array): Price Mechanism block gets 'Outline two effects of a price floor'; Indirect Taxes block gets 'Explain excess supply -> equilibrium'; the Assess and Evaluate questions are never surfaced.

2-per-step pairing leaves singleton steps that carry all block widgets: Block 1 = [how-markets, excess-demand] + [changes-in-equilibrium alone + diagram + quiz + practice + explain + takeaway]; Block 2 = [CS, PS] + [total-welfare alone + widgets]; Block 4 = [specific/ad-valorem, incidence] + [welfare-effects alone + widgets]. The heaviest steps are the ones with the least content, and the 'spaced' recall shown at the top of those steps is the previous step's weak reorder (e.g. the producer-surplus $150/$200 ordering).

Block 6 'Alternative Views of Consumer & Producer Behaviour' is misplaced: in the IAL spec it is 1.3.2(1b) 'Reasons why consumers may not aim to maximise utility' with a fixed list (herding, habitual behaviour, inertia, poor computational skills, need to feel valued, framing and bias). The block instead teaches anchoring, loss aversion, availability heuristic, nudges and Simon's bounded rationality, has no diagram, quiz or practice, and reads as an appendix.

Content weighting vs spec: two subsections on deadweight-loss welfare analysis (total-welfare-and-efficiency, welfare-effects-of-taxation) and one on the invisible hand are not IAL 1.3.4 bullets, while spec 3b (price mechanism in local, national and global markets) and 2b (how changes in demand/supply affect CS and PS) have no subsection at all.

Forward references: effects-and-evaluation-of-subsidies (body[0], recall) depends on 'positive externality' and 'socially optimal level', which are 1.3.5 concepts; total-welfare-and-efficiency introduces 'allocative efficiency' without the 1.3.5 framing.

Misconceptions: most are genuine (movement vs shift, CS is not 'saving', PS is not profit, ad valorem drawn parallel, subsidy shifts supply up, tax revenue is not a welfare loss, bounded rationality is not irrationality). Two are exam-technique tips dressed as misconceptions: signalling-incentive-rationing ('Students list the three functions but fail to explain') and behavioural-economics ('proves people are irrational').

Meta says mistakes: 0 but common_mistakes[] has 3 good entries (adjustment process, CS/PS labelling, marking the new equilibrium) - these are not surfaced in Learn Mode. Flashcards include price ceilings/floors/black markets (1.3.6 content).

Takeaways match their blocks and are accurate; difficulty ramp (equilibrium -> surplus -> mechanism -> tax -> subsidy) is sensible, with welfare tools introduced in Block 2 before being reused in Block 4.
1.3.4 3(b) The price mechanism in the context of different types of markets, including local, national and global markets - not taught anywhere (no subsection, no example, no recall, no MCQ).

1.3.4 2(b) How changes in demand or supply might affect consumer and producer surplus - only a one-line 'when price falls the triangle gets bigger'; no diagram of a shift's effect on CS/PS, and the one MCQ on it (Q14) is keyed 'ambiguous'.

1.3.4 4(d) The incidence of subsidies on consumers and producers - one sentence ('split depends on relative elasticities'); no rule stated (inelastic demand -> consumers capture more of the subsidy), no diagram, no recall; only Q20 tests it numerically.

1.3.4 4(a)/4(c) 'impact on... the government' - tax revenue rectangle and subsidy cost are stated in text/takeaways but never drawn; no Calculate practice on revenue or subsidy cost (IAL QS requirement).

1.3.2 1(b) (if Block 6 is kept here) - the spec list is herding, habitual behaviour, inertia, poor computational skills, the need to feel valued, framing and bias; the block teaches anchoring, loss aversion, availability heuristic, nudges and satisficing instead. Only 'poor computational skills' (via bounded rationality) and 'framing and bias' (via anchoring) are loosely covered.

Assessment format: nothing in the section is shaped like the WEC11 paper (Section A six 1-mark MCQs; Section B five short-answer questions totalling 20; Section C five-part data response of 34; Section D one 20-mark essay from a choice of two) or its command-word tariffs (Define 2, Calculate 2/4, Draw 4, Explain 4, Analyse 6, Examine 8, Discuss 14, Evaluate 20).

Remove the 10 off-topic GDP-measurement MCQs (indices 12-16, 18, 20-23) from this section's bank (move to 2.1.1) so the pre-test and inline quizzes only test what the section teaches; then re-point quizIndices so multiplier calculations (1, 3, 5) sit on block 4 and classification/equilibrium items (0, 4, 2/6, 9, 11) sit on blocks 1-3.

content.text: content[0] The Circular Flow of Income > three-sector-model > examMatters; and content[1] > injections-explained > body[0]: Teaches that transfer payments are government spending (G) and an injection ('these are government spending (injection) even though they are not payment for output'; 'Government spending (G) is expenditure on public services, infrastructure, and transfer payments'). Edexcel IAL treats G in AD as spending on goods and services and excludes transfer payments; quiz[13] in this very section says transfer payments are excluded from GDP. A student following the examMatters would lose the mark quiz[13] awards.

content.text: diagrams[0] main SVG 'Circular Flow of Income' and scenarios[1] 'Full Open Economy': The main diagram shows only the factor-services and factor-income arrows; there is no goods/services flow and no consumer-spending flow, so it fails the section's own examMatters ('label both the real flow and the money flow'). The open-economy scenario collapses 'Factor incomes / Consumer spending' onto one arrow in one direction. The checklist item 'Identify factor markets and product markets correctly' is not represented anywhere.

q2: Option B 'Aggregate demand equals aggregate supply' is treated as a distractor, but in IAL this IS the equilibrium condition for real national output, and quiz[10] in the same bank makes 'AD = AS, or equivalently injections equal withdrawals' the correct answer. Two correct options depending on which question the student saw last; only the phrase 'in the circular flow model' rescues it.
q13: Correct answer (excluded from GDP) contradicts the section body and examMatters, which call transfer payments government spending/an injection. Fix the content, not the question.

content.text: q12: Off-topic: GDP measurement methods are not taught anywhere in this section's content[] blocks, yet the question can be drawn into the 3-question pre-test. Same for indices 15, 16, 18, 21, 22, 23 (income method, NNI, PPP, real vs nominal, output method, GDP per capita) and 20 (stock vs flow). 10 of 24 MCQs test untaught material.
q1: Question is fine; placement is not. quizIndices for block 2 ('Injections and Withdrawals') = [1,2], so this multiplier calculation is the inline quiz two blocks before the multiplier is taught.

q3: Same sequencing problem: block 3 ('Equilibrium National Income') quizIndices = [3], so the second multiplier calculation is shown before block 4 teaches the multiplier. Meanwhile block 4's inline quiz is quiz[4] (basic I/G/X vs S/T/M classification) — too easy for the multiplier block — and quiz[5] (which factor shrinks the multiplier) is never shown because only the first unused index is used.

p1: 'Explain two reasons why national income figures may not accurately reflect the standard of living (6 marks)' — this is 2.1.1 (measures of economic performance / limitations of GDP), not circular flow / equilibrium / multiplier. Because practice is sorted by marks in LearnModeTab.jsx:80, this lands as the inline practice for block 3 'Equilibrium National Income' where it is irrelevant.

content.text: p-1: No practice question requires a diagram (J/W or AD/AS) or a multiplier calculation with given MPS/MPT/MPM, which are the two most common ways IAL Unit 2 tests this topic.

Heavy redundancy: content[0] section 'three-sector-model' already teaches all three injections, all three withdrawals and the J = W equilibrium rule in full; content[1] then re-teaches 'Injections: I, G, X', 'Withdrawals: S, T, M' and 'The Injections-Withdrawals Balance' as three separate sections. A student reads the same takeaway ('Injections (I, G, X) add to the flow; withdrawals (S, T, M) leak out') at the end of block 1 and again at the end of block 2.

content[2] 'planned-vs-actual' and 'adjustment-to-equilibrium' are the same mechanism told twice (excess demand → inventories fall; excess supply → inventories rise). Merge into one section with both directions and use the freed slot for the AD/AS equilibrium diagram the spec expects.

Broken diagramRefs: content[2].diagramRef = 'National Income Equilibrium' and content[3].diagramRef = 'The Multiplier' match no diagram title ('Circular Flow of Income', 'Injections and Withdrawals Equilibrium') under the bidirectional substring match in LearnModeTab.jsx:97-104. Blocks 3 and 4 therefore render no InlineDiagram; the J/W diagram with its 'ΔY > ΔJ' multiplier scenario is shown at block 2, before the multiplier exists.

Inline quiz sequencing (quizIndices): block 2 → quiz[1] (multiplier calc), block 3 → quiz[3] (multiplier calc), block 4 → quiz[4] (basic classification). Calculations appear two blocks before the concept; the multiplier block gets the easiest question; quiz[2] and quiz[5] are never surfaced.

Pre-test draws 3 random MCQs from a 24-item bank in which 10 items test GDP-measurement content (2.1.1) never taught in this section — a plausible driver of the 'pre-test demotivates' feedback and of step-0 abandonment.

content.text: Step pairing: block 2 (3 sections) and block 4 (3 sections) leave a single-section final step carrying diagram + quiz + practice + explain-back + takeaway + two recall widgets — the heaviest step in the section is anchored by the shortest content. Block 1 and 3 (2 sections each) are one step each, so the section has 6 steps but 4 block-end widget dumps.
Takeaways match their blocks, but content[0].takeaway[1-2] duplicate content[1].takeaway[0-2] almost verbatim.

Misconceptions: 'savings as injection / investment as withdrawal', 'investment vs financial investment', 'I = S, G = T, X = M must each hold', 'identity vs equilibrium', 'multiplier is a fixed number', and 'MPC must exclude tax/imports' are genuine and well-phrased. 'Students treat the circular flow as a description of reality' and 'Students describe the adjustment as instantaneous' are filler — not errors students actually make in exams.

Difficulty ramp inside prose is sensible (model → J/W → equilibrium → multiplier → evaluation), but the section never connects to AD/AS: the multiplier is not explicitly linked to the size of an AD shift (spec bullet), and 'equilibrium real national output' is only shown via J/W and Keynesian-cross narrative, never on price-level/real-output axes.

Distinction between income and wealth (flow vs stock) — quiz[20] tests it but no content[] section teaches it (unsure whether IAL keeps the UK 2.4.1 wording, but it appears in IAL textbooks for this topic).

content.text: Equilibrium level of real national output shown on an AD/AS diagram (price level vs real output) and using AD/AS to show how the economy moves toward equilibrium — no AD/AS diagram or explanation in this section; equilibrium is treated only through injections/withdrawals and the inventory mechanism.
Significance of the multiplier for shifts in AD (the multiplied horizontal shift of AD) — only implied by quiz[8]; not taught in content[3].

The multiplier ratio as change in real income / change in injection, with calculations from given data (e.g. given ΔY and ΔG, find k) — only the k = 1/MPW direction is drilled; the ratio definition appears only in notes[3] and practice[2] guidance.

Note: the app numbers this 2.3.4 and the notes cross-reference 2.3.2 (AD), 2.3.5 (output gap), 2.3.6 (fiscal policy); I am unsure this matches the official WEC12 numbering (UK GCE uses 2.4 for national income) — worth verifying the spec mapping across the whole unit.

Repair the block-level wiring: set quizIndices by topic (e.g. block2 → [12,18,21,23], block4 → [5,13,17,9], block5 → [2,22], block6 → [4,7,14,16,19,20], block7 → [6,8,15,24]), point practiceIndices so the 6/10/14-mark questions appear on the matching blocks, add diagramRef 'CPI Basket' to block 3 and 'Types of Unemployment' to block 6, and build an AD/AS diagram (axes: price level / real output) for block 4 so its diagramRef resolves.

Replace the four non-orderable/arbitrary reorders (factor incomes, CPI-vs-RPI differences, ILO criteria, HDI components) with matching/classification exercises, and give fill-ins distractor words plus numeric calculation blanks (real GDP, per-capita, weighted CPI, value added) instead of three-word banks with letter hints.

Close the spec gaps most likely to be examined in WEC12: add an 'Effects of unemployment' subsection, money-supply growth as an inflation cause, 'Limitations of the CPI' (replacing most of RPI-vs-CPI), real-wage unemployment, and a short capital/financial account explainer; swap several UK examples for Asian/Middle-East ones.

Fix the practice set to WEC12 tariffs and marking: Define = 2 marks, drop 'Outline' for 'Explain', convert the 20-mark Evaluate into a 14-mark Discuss (or label it Unit 4 style), and rewrite the 10/14-mark schemes as levels (KAA + Evaluation) rather than point tallies.

Correct the factual slips: Q3 explanation (CPIH does not include mortgage interest; RPI does), 'CPI excludes housing costs', GNI 'citizens' → residents, US CA 'every year since 1982', 2023 RPI–CPI gap and rail-fare claim, the unverified ONS 2024 basket example, and reframe 2021-22 US inflation and the 1930s New Deal claim as mixed/contested.

q3: Explanation states 'CPI does NOT include mortgage interest payments (that's CPIH)'. Wrong: CPIH adds owner-occupiers' housing costs via rental equivalence, not mortgage interest; it is the RPI that includes mortgage interest payments. Also 'substitution bias' (the key) is never taught anywhere in the content, so the pre-test/inline draw can present an untaught concept.

p0: 'Define the term GDP (4 marks)' — in IAL Economics 'Define' items carry 2 marks; the scheme awards marks for the three measurement methods, real vs nominal, and 'most widely used indicator', none of which a define mark scheme credits. Teaches students to pad definitions. This is also the item that surfaces inside the Inflation block in Learn Mode (practiceIndices [0] → sortedPractice[0]).

p3: 'Evaluate... (20 marks)' — WEC12 (Unit 2) papers have no 20-mark essay; the top tariff is 14 ('Discuss') with 12 'Assess'. 20-mark 'Evaluate' is a WEC13/WEC14 format. The scheme is also point-tallied (2+3+2+2+3+2+2+2+2) whereas IAL marks 10+ questions on KAA/Evaluation levels, so the 'model answer' misrepresents how marks are earned.

Inline quiz mapping is broken: block.quizIndices are simply [0],[1],...,[7] and LearnModeTab.jsx:106-108 uses them literally, so block 2 'Uses and Limitations of GDP' shows Q2 (malign deflation), block 4 'Inflation: Causes and Effects' shows Q4 (structural unemployment coal miner), block 5 'Deflation' shows Q5 (cost-push oil), block 6 'Employment and Unemployment' shows Q6 (UK current account), block 7 'Current Account' shows Q7 (LFS vs claimant count). Only blocks 0, 1 and 3 get a topically relevant MCQ.

No diagram ever renders in Learn Mode: block 4 diagramRef 'Demand-Pull and Cost-Push Inflation' matches neither stored diagram title ('CPI Basket of Goods', 'Types of Unemployment') under the substring test at LearnModeTab.jsx:97-104, and blocks 3 and 6 (which those diagrams fit) have diagramRef null. The section has no AD/AS diagram at all, yet demand-pull and cost-push examMatters both instruct students to shift AD/SRAS on a diagram (and never state the axes: price level / real output).

Inline practice mapping: block 4 (Inflation) practiceIndices [0] resolves to sortedPractice[0] = 'Define GDP (4 marks)'; block 6 → 'Outline two types of unemployment' (correct). P1, P2, P3 (the 6/10/20-mark items) never surface in Learn Mode, so students never meet an Assess/Evaluate question in the guided flow.

Every block has exactly 3 sections, so 2-per-step pairing yields [s1,s2] then a lone [s3] step that also carries diagram+quiz+practice+ExplainItBack+takeaway — 16 steps with an uneven 'light, heavy' rhythm. Recall scheduling side-effect (LearnModeTab.jsx:345-359, 397-402): the lone section's recall is shown as 'immediate' at the bottom of its step and again as 'spaced' at the top of the very next step, i.e. 8 recalls (gdp-per-capita, expenditure-method, HDI, measuring-inflation, effects-of-inflation, consequences-of-deflation, causes-and-policies, current-account-surplus) appear twice back-to-back while the middle section's recall appears once and nothing is actually spaced.

recall.shuffled uses only two permutations across all 12 reorders ([2,0,3,1] ×7 and [3,1,0,2] ×5); ReorderRecall.jsx:9 applies them verbatim, so the displayed order is predictable and a student can learn 'swap positions' patterns.

Fill-in word banks are exactly the three answers (FillInRecall.jsx:12), so all 12 fill-ins are 3-item drag-drops with grammatically forced slots; combined with letter-count hints they cannot discriminate understanding.

Terminology drift between layers: content teaches 'demand-side / supply-side deflation', quiz Q2 tests 'malign / benign'; content teaches real GDP via base-year prices, quiz Q1/Q10 test the GDP deflator formula; content never mentions substitution bias but Q3 keys on it. The pre-test draws randomly from all 25, so the gate can be failed on untaught material (consistent with the founder's 'pre-test demotivates' hypothesis).

Sequencing/scope: HDI (Unit 4 development in IAL) sits inside the GDP-limitations block; the Deflation block spends a full subsection on liquidity trap and QE (policy, later units) while the Unemployment block omits the effects/costs of unemployment entirely, so block depth is inverted relative to the spec.

Takeaways match their blocks well and misconceptions are largely genuine student errors (GDP=wealth; disinflation=deflation; deficit always bad; cutting rates always fixes deflation). Two are filler: 'cost-push inflation only comes from oil prices' and 'GDP is useless'.

Difficulty ramp is flat rather than rising: every subsection follows the same template (definition, flow, example, misconception) with no calculation practice until the quiz, so the numeracy the spec demands (index numbers, real growth, per-capita, weighted CPI) is never scaffolded in the notes.
Effects/costs of unemployment on consumers, firms, workers, government and society — entirely absent (block 6 covers measurement, types and policies only).
Growth of the money supply as a cause of inflation — not mentioned (IAL 2.3.1 lists demand-pull, cost-push and money supply growth).
Limitations of the CPI as a measure of inflation (substitution bias, quality change, representative household, basket lag, sampling) — not taught, though tested in Q3 and practice P2.
Effects of inflation on the government and on firms' competitiveness/investment in depth — only savers/borrowers/workers covered; government (fiscal drag, debt erosion, tax revenue) missing.

Real-wage inflexibility (classical) unemployment and the significance of migration and skills for employment — not taught; the 'cutting wages' misconception dismisses the real-wage view rather than explaining it.
Employment rate, economic inactivity rate and the significance of changes in them; underemployment gets a single bullet.
Capital and financial accounts as the counterpart to the current account — mentioned only in passing as the financing source; no structure of the BoP.
Relationship between current account imbalances and other macro objectives, and interconnectedness of economies through trade — not taught.

Value vs volume, index numbers and calculating rates of change/growth from data (a core WEC12 data-response skill) — no worked calculations in the notes; the deflator formula appears only in the quiz.
Weighted-average construction of the CPI with a numerical example — process described in words only.
Unsure: whether IAL 2.3.1 names RPI/CPIH or HDI at all; both are covered here in depth and may be over-coverage of UK-GCE material rather than gaps.

Fix Learn Mode wiring: set diagramRef strings that substring-match the diagram titles ('The AD Curve' for block 2, reuse its shift scenarios for block 3, 'The Multiplier Effect' for block 4) and reassign quizIndices by topic (block 3 -> Q4/Q12/Q16, block 4 -> Q3/Q21/Q24, block 5 -> Q7/Q15) so students stop seeing a multiplier calculation before the multiplier is taught. Also route the 10- and 20-mark practice items into Learn Mode.

Correct the content errors: consumption is NOT the most volatile component (determinants-of-consumption keyIdea); rewrite the 2022-inflation example so BoE rate rises are a shift, not the 'interest rate effect'; fix the car-industry accelerator example (sales fell); replace 'narrowly avoided a recession'; use one currency per example and fix '80p of every extra $1'; align the multiplier formula teaching with Q21.

Replace the 10 non-genuine recalls with application exercises: movement-vs-shift classifier (movements-along-ad), C/I/G/X-M classifier (ad-formula), MPW->k calculation comparison (multiplier-size-determinants), numeric accelerator table (accelerator-definition), scenario-based limitation matcher (limitations); drop leading-letter hints everywhere.

Remove or shrink the duplicated multiplier block (it lives in 2.3.4 national-income with overlapping ids) and use the space for missing 2.3.2 spec bullets: saving vs consumption and MPC/MPS, gross vs net investment, animal spirits and access to credit in the investment body, G over the trade cycle, protectionism and non-price factors for net trade. Cut the accelerator to one subsection.

Rebuild practice to IAL format: Define (2), Explain (4/6), Analyse (8) with a diagram, Assess (10/12), Evaluate (20) with levels-based guidance that sums correctly; add a short data extract and a 'Calculate the multiplier / change in national income' item; strip Marshall-Lerner and J-curve from the WEC12 mark scheme. While there, swap most UK-only examples (and Q8's NHS/JSA) for country-neutral or Asian/Middle-East cases to match the audience.

Components of Aggregate Demand > determinants-of-consumption > keyIdea: States consumption 'is the largest and most volatile component of AD'. Investment is the most volatile component (as the next subsection's keyIdea, the block takeaway 'Investment is the most volatile', and block 5's takeaway all say). Consumption is the largest and the most stable. Direct internal contradiction on a fact IAL examiners test.
